read.sections.0.text.note: Crop and place names: lúa mì, lúa mạch, kê, chuối, khoai môn, ngô, đậu, khoai tây, cao lương; 'Niu Ghi-nê' for New Guinea (usual name for the island is also 'New Guinea'; contested/political risk is low but check), 'Mexico', 'dãy Andes'. Reviewer: check each crop name.
read.sections.0.text.source: For most of human history, people got their food by foraging. They gathered wild plants, hunted animals and caught fish. More than 10,000 years ago, some groups began to plant seeds and keep animals. Farming did not start in just one place or at one time, and different parts of the world grew different crops. Farmers in West Asia grew wheat and barley, while farmers in China grew rice and millet. People in New Guinea grew bananas and taro, and people in Mexico grew maize and beans. People in the Andes mountains first farmed potatoes, and people in parts of Africa first farmed sorghum. In Harapan Valley, one group still moves around to find food, while the other group farms.
read.sections.0.text.back: For most of human history, people got food by hunting and gathering. They gathered wild plants, hunted animals and caught fish. More than 10,000 years ago, some groups began to sow seeds and raise animals. Farming did not begin in only one place or at one moment, and each region of the world grew different crops. Farmers in West Asia grew wheat and barley, while farmers in China grew rice and millet. People in New Guinea grew bananas and taro, while people in Mexico grew maize and beans. People in the Andes were the first to grow potatoes, and people in some parts of Africa were the first to grow sorghum. In Harapan Valley, one group still moved around to find food, while the other group farmed.

read.sections.0.simpler.note: 'Ngũ cốc' for grain; 'các loại ngũ cốc khác' stands for 'other grains' (sorghum).
read.sections.0.simpler.source: Long ago, people got food by foraging. They picked wild plants and caught fish. More than 10,000 years ago, some groups began to farm. They planted seeds and kept animals. Farming began in many places at different times. Each place had its own crops. West Asia grew wheat, and China grew rice. Mexico grew corn. Parts of Africa grew other grains. In Harapan Valley, one group moves to find food. The other group farms.
read.sections.0.simpler.back: Long ago, people got food by hunting and gathering. They gathered wild plants and caught fish. More than 10,000 years ago, some groups began to farm. They sowed seeds and raised animals. Farming began in many places, at different times. Each place had its own crops. West Asia grew wheat, while China grew rice. Mexico grew maize. Some parts of Africa grew other grains. In Harapan Valley, one group went from place to place to find food. The other group farmed.

read.sections.1.text.note: 'Chuyên làm một việc' for 'specialise' (KEY_TERMS says hard to say simply); 'phần dư' for surplus; 'trao đổi' vs 'đổi lấy' vs 'buôn bán' for trade: I used 'trao đổi' because the lesson is about swapping pots for grain. Check this reads as 'trade' to a 12-year-old. | Review: 'bội thu' (bumper harvest) is used for English 'good harvest' here, in the table, glossary example and write example: slightly stronger than the English; 'được mùa' / 'vụ mùa tốt' may be more neutral. Also 'phần dư' glossary term and 'chuyên làm một việc' (KEY_TERMS asked for a check).
read.sections.1.text.source: Farming could grow a lot of food in a small area. After a good harvest, a village might have a surplus, which is more food than people need right away. With extra grain in store, not everyone had to farm, so some people could specialise in making pots, cloth or tools. In Harapan Valley, one family makes clay pots and gives them to farmers in exchange for grain. This is a kind of trade. Villages also traded with each other, and a village near the sea might trade salt for grain. Over time, some farming villages grew into towns.
read.sections.1.text.back: Farming can produce a lot of food on a small area. After a bumper harvest, a village may have a surplus, meaning more food than everyone needs right then. When there is extra grain in storage, not everyone needs to farm, so some people can specialise in one job, such as making pots, weaving cloth or making tools. In Harapan Valley, one family made clay pots and gave them to the farmers in exchange for grain. This is a form of exchange. Villages also exchanged with each other, and a village near the sea might swap salt for grain. Over time, some farming villages grew into towns.

read.sections.1.simpler.note: 'Họ đưa nồi và nhận ngũ cốc' for 'They give pots and get grain'; check natural. | Review: 'phần dư, tức là thức ăn thừa': 'thừa' can suggest waste; check.
read.sections.1.simpler.source: A farm can grow lots of food in a small space. After a good year, there may be a surplus of extra food. People keep it safe for later. Now not everyone has to farm, so some people can specialise. They do one main job, like making pots. In Harapan Valley, one family makes pots. They give pots and get grain. This is trade. Villages trade with each other too, and some grow into towns.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: A small piece of land can give a lot of food. After a good year, there may be a surplus, meaning leftover food. People store it for later. Now not everyone needs to farm, so some people can specialise in one job, such as making pots. In Harapan Valley, one family made pots. They gave pots and received grain. This is exchange. Villages also exchanged with each other, and some villages grew into towns.

read.sections.2.text.note: 'Vụ mùa thất bát' (harvest fails), 'nạn đói' elsewhere. 'Quyền lực' for power. Check sensitive content stays factual and short. | Review: 'tích trữ ngũ cốc' can read as hoarding (English: 'stored grain'); native reviewer to decide if too negative.
read.sections.2.text.source: Farming was hard work, with long days of planting, watering and harvesting. Many villages depended on only a few crops. If the rain did not come, the harvest could fail and people had little to eat. Living close to animals and to many other people also helped some illnesses spread. In some places, a few families took control of more land and stored grain, which gave them more power. Not every group chose to farm, and many kept foraging or did some of both. So historians ask a careful question: was farming better, and better for whom?
read.sections.2.text.back: Farming is hard work, with long days of sowing, watering and harvesting. Many villages relied on just a few crops. If the rain did not come, the harvest could fail and people had very little to eat. Living close to livestock and close to many other people also made some diseases spread more easily. In some places, a few families controlled more land and hoarded grain, which gave them more power. Not every group chose to farm; many groups kept hunting and gathering or did both. So historians ask a careful question: was farming better, and better for whom?

read.sections.2.simpler.source: Farming is hard work. Many villages grow only a few crops. If no rain comes, the crops can die. Then there is not much to eat. People live close to animals and to each other, so sickness can spread. Some families get more land and food. This gives them more power. Not every group chooses to farm. Many keep foraging. So we ask: was farming better? Who was it better for?
read.sections.2.simpler.back: Farming is hard work. Many villages grew only a few crops. If there was no rain, the plants could die. Then there was not much to eat. People lived close to livestock and to each other, so disease spread easily. Some families had more land and food. This gave them more power. Not every group chose to farm. Many groups still hunted and gathered. So we ask: is farming better? Better for whom?

write.example.source: Farming helped people because it could grow a lot of food in one place. One example from the lesson is the farming village in Harapan Valley. After a good harvest, it has a surplus of grain. This lets one family specialise in making pots. But farming also brought a problem: the village grows only a few crops. If the rain does not come, the whole harvest can fail. This was hard for families with no extra land or grain. So I think farming was important, but it was not better for everyone.
write.example.back: Farming helped people because it could produce a lot of food in one place. One example from the lesson is the farming village in Harapan Valley. After a bumper harvest, the village had a surplus of grain. This let one family specialise in one job: making pots. But farming also brought a problem: the village grew only a few crops. If the rain did not come, the whole harvest could fail. This was hard for families who had no extra land or grain. So I think farming was very important, but not better for everyone.

watch.summary.source: This video explains why farming was such a big change in human history. For a very long time, people found their food in the wild. Then people in several parts of the world began to grow crops and keep animals. Farming could make more food in a smaller area. So more people could live in one place, and villages could grow. Stored food let some people do other work, like making tools or trading. Some people became leaders. Farming also changed the land around people. But farming brought risks too. A bad harvest could mean hunger. Illness could spread more easily. Some people got much more land and power than others. Farming was very important, but it did not make life better for everyone in the same way.
watch.summary.back: This video explains why farming was a big change in human history. For a very long time, people found food in the wild. Then people in many places around the world began to grow plants and raise animals. Farming can produce more food on a smaller area. So more people can live in one place, and villages can grow. Stored food helps some people do other jobs, such as making tools or trading. Some people became leaders. Farming also changed the land around people. But farming also had risks. A failed harvest can cause famine. Disease can spread more easily. Some people had much more land and power than others. Farming was very important, but it did not make life better for everyone in the same way.
